title: Astrophotography Basics

cards.b: Your eye collects very little light, so it cannot see colours or faint nebulae well. A camera can collect light for minutes. That is why almost every famous sky picture is a long exposure, and why learning the basics makes you a better observer too.

The sky turns about 15 degrees every hour because Earth rotates. A long exposure of stars on a fixed tripod therefore shows trails. The 500 rule is a rough guide: divide 500 by your lens focal length in millimetres to get the longest exposure in seconds before trails appear.

Each short exposure carries random noise. Averaging many frames cancels that noise, roughly in proportion to the square root of the number of frames. Astronomers call this stacking. Professional images are made this way, with hundreds of frames combined. Stacking also lets software reject satellite trails and hot pixels, which appear in only some of the frames.

A small motorised mount that turns at the sidereal rate cancels Earth's rotation. This lets exposures run for many minutes without trails. Equatorial mounts are built with their axis parallel to Earth's, pointing at the celestial pole. Many amateurs use a simple equatorial mount because it turns about one axis, which keeps stars fixed in the frame.

Many deep-sky pictures are taken through filters that pass one glowing gas at a time, such as hydrogen-alpha red. The images are then combined, and colours are chosen to show different gases. Hubble's famous pictures use this same approach, so many "colours" are assigned. Hubble images are often released in false colour, and the colour choice is both a scientific and an artistic decision.

Use a wide lens, a fast aperture around f/2.8, a high ISO such as 1600 to 3200, and manual focus set on a bright star. Shoot raw files so you keep the faint detail. Keep batteries warm in cold nights, because cold drains them fast.

cards.h: How the first sky photos worked
cards.b: In 1880, Henry Draper photographed the Orion Nebula with a long exposure, one of the first astronomical photographs of a nebula. Photographic plates, not eyes, revealed many faint objects for the first time, and they were measured for decades before digital sensors took over. Those plates recorded faint stars that eyes could not hold, and some of the early records they made of changing stars are still used.

• 'A phone photo of the Moon is useless.' It is a fine start; the Moon is bright enough for short exposures.
  • 'More megapixels make better sky photos.' Light collected and dark current matter more.
  • 'Pictures show the real colours.' Most deep-sky colours are assigned by the photographer.

The Indian Institute of Astrophysics runs the Himalayan Chandra Telescope (2.01 m) at Hanle in Ladakh, where high, dry, dark skies give sharp images. Amateur clubs across India share astrophotos through national astronomy societies, and many students now start with a basic camera and a tripod.

• Long exposures collect light the eye cannot.
  • The 500 rule limits trails for untracked shots.
  • Stacking many frames cuts random noise.
  • Deep-sky colours are often assigned from filtered data.
